128.title: Top Card
128.text: Welcome to the Info system, a small reference about ants and about playing the game. Press a topic box to open its page. The Previous button steps back to the page you saw before, and the Top button brings you back here. Words shown in *highlighted* type are special: press and hold the mouse button on one to see what it means.

130.title: Ant anatomy
130.text: Look at an ant and you will find three body regions: a head at the front, a thorax in the middle and an abdomen at the rear. Press a box to read about each one. The body is covered by a hard shell of *chitin*, which works as a skeleton on the outside. Ants breathe through tiny air tubes instead of lungs. They have no ears either, but detectors in the head, thorax and legs pick up the vibrations of the ground.

131.title: Head
131.text: The head carries the antennae, the eyes, the mouthparts and the brain. The brain is tiny, yet an ant can learn and remember for a long time: it may still know the way to a food source after a whole winter in the nest. Press a box to read more about the eyes, the antennae and the mouth, or to see what the ocelli and the maxillae are.

132.title: Thorax
132.text: All six legs are attached to the thorax, the part of the body between the head and the abdomen. Each leg ends in a foot with a pair of curved claws, which give a grip for climbing walls and for walking upside down. A front leg also has a cleaning comb, a notch lined with bristles; the ant draws an antenna or a leg through it to clean it.

133.title: Abdomen
133.text: The abdomen is the rear section of the body. It begins with a narrow waist, the petiole, and goes on with the gaster. The gaster holds the *crop* for stored food, the intestine and the glands that make scent signals and other chemical messages. Some ants have a sting at the tip. Press a box to read about the parts inside.

158.title: Eyes
158.text: The compound eye of an ant is made of many tiny lenses, called facets. Ants that hunt by sight have large eyes and see quite well, and many that live underground still have tiny ones. Ants see moving things better than still ones, which is why a foraging ant stops and looks about between short walks. On top of the head some ants have three simple eyes, the *ocelli*, which only tell light from dark.

159.title: Antennae
159.text: The antennae are an ant's main sense organs, used for touch, smell and the sensing of vibrations. Each antenna is elbowed and has two parts: a long first part, the scape, and a segmented part beyond the elbow, the funiculus, which carries the sense organs. The antennae are never still: the ant keeps waving them about. The two of them compare the strength of a smell, which tells the ant what direction it comes from, and an ant that loses one antenna loses that skill.

160.title: Mouth
160.text: The mandibles are an ant's jaws, and they bite sideways, like pincers. Ants use them to fight, to dig and to carry things. Behind them are the smaller *maxillae*, which help to chew and also clean the legs and antennae. Chewed food is kept in the *infrabuccal* pocket beneath the mouth opening, where muscles squeeze the juice out of it. The ant swallows the juice, which is then held in the *crop*, and throws away the dry leftovers.

134.title: Social insects
134.text: Many insects live and work in groups, because a group can do things that one animal alone cannot. The four big groups of social insects are ants, termites, bees and wasps. What marks a society? Its members stay together, and they are divided into different kinds, each belonging to a *caste* with its own job. Individuals give up their own interests for the good of the group. Some spiders show a milder form of group life.

135.title: Ants
135.text: Of all the social insects, ants are found in the most places and in the greatest numbers. There are more kinds of ant than of all the other social insects put together, and they live in places as different as deserts, forests, grasslands and city streets. Their colonies range from a few dozen ants to millions, and they live on every continent except Antarctica. Ants descend from wasp-like ancestors. The oldest fossil ants are found in amber about a hundred million years old, and they still show some wasp features.

136.title: Termites
136.text: Termites are small, soft-bodied social insects. They look like ants but belong to a different group, and they probably descend from cockroach-like ancestors. Their colonies have *castes* that include both males and females. Most termites eat wood, with the help of microbes in their gut. Some build mounds of earth taller than a person. Unlike an ant colony, a termite colony has a king as well as a queen. Because they stay inside the nest almost all the time, nearly all are blind. Nasute soldiers are a special *caste*: from a snout on the head they squirt a sticky fluid at their enemies.

137.title: Bees
137.text: There are thousands of kinds of bee. They gather nectar and pollen, and most are hairy, winged and able to sting. Most bees live alone. Only a minority, such as honeybees and bumblebees, are social, and a social bee colony has three *castes*: drones, workers and queens. Honeybees live in hives of wax comb. Press the Next button to read more about bees.

179.title: Bees 2
179.text: A foraging bee collects pollen on the hairs of its hind legs and carries it to the hive, where it feeds the *larvae*. Bees also tell their nestmates where food is by dancing: the waggle dance shows the direction and distance of the flowers. Bees turn the nectar they bring home into honey. Bees matter to people too, because they pollinate many of our crops.

138.title: Wasps
138.text: Most wasps live alone. Taken together, wasps show every step from solitary to fully social life, which helps scientists to study how social life began. Many solitary wasps paralyse a spider or a caterpillar and store it for their young. Social wasps build nests of paper. The adults drink nectar, but they feed their *larvae* on chewed-up insects.

139.title: Castes
139.text: An ant society contains ants of different body forms, each with its own job. These groups are called *castes*, and the colony needs all of them to survive. The queen lays just two sorts of egg: one gives females and the other males. At the start all the female eggs are alike. How the larva is fed and tended settles its final form: a new queen, a soldier or a worker. Press a name in the menu to read about each caste.

140.title: Worker
140.text: Workers, which are sterile females, make up most of a colony. They dig, look after the *brood*, gather food, share it with the queen and their hungry nestmates, and fight when the nest is attacked. A worker lives about a year, and in a few species several years. Some workers keep one job all their lives, while others change jobs as they get older.

141.title: Soldier
141.text: Soldiers are sterile females, larger than the workers, with oversized heads and powerful mandibles. The big head is mostly muscle for working the jaws, not a bigger brain. In some species the soldiers have flat, plug-shaped heads, and they seal the nest entrance with them. A soldier steps aside only when an ant coming back from *foraging* gives the correct signal. Soldiers are also called major workers, and the small workers are called minor workers.

142.title: Replete
142.text: In some ants, above all in dry climates, certain workers fill their crops with liquid food until they swell so much that they cannot walk. They hang in the nest as living larders, which helps the colony to survive dry spells. The honeypot ants of Australia and North America are well-known examples. When food is scarce, their nestmates are fed by them through *trophallaxis*, the sharing of liquid food from mouth to mouth.

143.title: Male
143.text: Males belong to the shortest-lived *caste*, and some live only a few weeks. They do no work and exist only to mate. Most have wings, which they use on the mating flight. Compared with a worker, a male has a small head and large eyes.

144.title: New queen
144.text: New queens are winged, fertile females, usually much larger than the workers, that leave on the mating flight. After mating, a queen may return to her own nest, join another colony or found a new one. To found one she must avoid being eaten, find shelter and rub off her wings. She digs a tiny chamber and seals herself in. There she lives on the reserves of her own body, even her wing muscles, until her first workers have grown up and bring in food. Until then she raises the first *brood* alone.

145.title: Queen
145.text: Once her colony is founded, the queen's main task is to lay eggs. A colony may have one queen or many, even thousands. A queen is larger than her workers, and the workers feed and groom her. In some species she lays thousands of eggs in a day. No other *caste* lives as long as the queens, and some of them survive for over twenty years. A queen keeps the sperm she received for years in a special organ. Fertilised eggs become females; only at certain times does she lay unfertilised eggs, which become males.

146.title: Behavior
146.text: Ant behavior fascinates scientists and children alike. Each ant does simple things, yet together the ants of a colony do surprisingly complex ones. Nobody gives orders. The *castes* specialise in different jobs, but any ant can pass a message to any other ant. Press a name in the menu to read about eight kinds of behavior.

147.title: Nest building
147.text: Ants live in very different places, so they build very different homes: tunnels in the ground, a few reaching deeper than a tall person, mounds above ground, nests under stones, in trees and plants, in walls and in the foundations of houses. Press a box to read about the queen or the young, or to learn what a room of the nest is for.

148.title: Communication
148.text: A colony works only if its members can pass on information. Ant signals are simpler than human speech, yet they are enough. Ants use touches, strokes and taps, sounds made by rubbing body parts together (stridulation), grasping, nudging and tasting. Above all they use chemical signals, the *pheromones*. Press the Antennae box to read about the organs that sense them.

149.title: Scent trails
149.text: A forager that finds food walks home slowly, dragging the tip of its gaster along the ground to mark a trail with *pheromones*. Other ants follow the trail, and each ant that returns with food adds more scent. The trail grows stronger and draws still more ants. When the food is used up, the ants stop adding scent, the scent fades away and the trail is soon forgotten.

163.title: Food sharing
163.text: Ants pass liquid food from mouth to mouth, a habit called *trophallaxis*. An ant that has gone out to *forage* comes home with a full *crop*. Only what the ant itself needs goes on to be digested. The rest belongs to the colony's common supply, and it is passed on whenever two ants meet and touch antennae. In this way food reaches ants that never leave the nest, such as the queen and the young. A hungry ant begs for a share by tapping with its antennae and front legs.

164.title: Brood care
164.text: A worker carries each egg to a nursery chamber. Eggs need steady warmth and humidity, so the nurse workers move the *brood* between chambers all day long, to keep it near the right temperature, which is about 25 degrees Celsius. They also lick the eggs clean, and the nurses feed the larvae too.

150.title: Fighting
150.text: Workers as well as soldiers will fight to the death for their colony, and ants know strangers by their smell. Many ants also bite hard with their mandibles, and some species spray formic acid from the tip of the gaster. Their other weapons are poisons and secretions, which are sprayed, squirted or rubbed onto the enemy. Some species even use scent signals, or *pheromones*, to confuse the enemy.

151.title: Herding aphids
151.text: *Aphids* drink plant sap and squirt out the surplus as *honeydew*. Some ants stroke the aphids, which is called milking, to collect it. In return, the ants keep other insects away from their herd. Some ants even carry aphids to fresh plants.

170.title: Foraging
170.text: Foragers often travel far from the nest and still find their way home again. In the usual pattern of *foraging*, scouts, often older workers, search for food, wandering at random until they find something. Food small enough is carried home by the ant alone. A bigger find makes the scout lay a chemical trail back to the nest and *recruit* others to help. Food too big for one ant is cut up and carried home by several.

152.title: Common species
152.text: Well over ten thousand kinds of ant are known, and many more have not yet been found, so these cards show only a sample of common and interesting ones. Some of them you may have met in your own garden or home. Press a name in the menu to read about one of six kinds.

153.title: Weaver ants
153.text: Weaver ants live in Africa, southern Asia and Australia. Many workers form living chains that draw leaves towards each other. Other workers grip nearly grown *larvae* in their jaws and use the sticky silk the larvae spin as glue to join the leaves into a nest in the trees. A single colony may have several nests, in many trees. The workers bite hard, and they can spray a sharp-smelling acid at intruders.

154.title: Harvester ants
154.text: Harvester ants live in dry regions and mostly eat seeds, though they also take insects and fruit. Their nests are deep and elaborate, some reaching more than two metres down, with chambers where the seeds are stored. Workers carry the seeds home in their jaws, and some species clear the ground bare around the nest entrance.

155.title: Army ants
155.text: Army ants are hunters that wander. Two well-known kinds are the legionary ants, from tropical America, and the driver ants, which live in Africa. Their life has two phases. In the nomadic phase the colony moves on every day, carrying its *brood* along and hunting on the way. In the stationary phase the ants gather in a camp, the bivouac, where the wingless queen lays her eggs.

156.title: Leafcutter ants
156.text: Leafcutter ants are farmers. Workers cut leaves and flowers and carry them to the nest. There the smaller workers chew them into a pulp. The pulp feeds a fungus that the ants grow underground, and the fungus is their main food. The pieces of leaf are carried held high over the head, in long lines along worn trails. A mature colony can hold millions of ants.

165.title: Carpenter ants
165.text: Carpenter ants are the best-known wood-nesting ants. They nest in rotten logs and trees, and sometimes in wooden buildings. They chew tunnels through soft, rotten wood but, unlike termites, they do not eat it.

166.title: Fire ants
166.text: Fire ants are small reddish ants from South America. A colony may have hundreds of thousands of ants. They hold on with their jaws while they sting, and the sting is painful. Fire ants were accidentally brought to the southern United States early in the twentieth century, and they have been spreading ever since, by a few miles each year.

157.title: Life cycle
157.text: A colony can be seen like any living thing: it is born, grows, matures and reproduces. It can also be seen in terms of energy, which means food. The colony grows and stores energy. Once it is mature, it spends some of it on reproduction, in the form of new queens and males. This point comes at very different sizes, from a few dozen ants to hundreds of thousands. Press a box to read about the life cycle of an ant or of a colony.

161.title: Ant life cycle
161.text: Young and adult ants look completely different. A queen lays tens to hundreds of eggs a day, and a worker carries each egg to a nursery. After about two weeks the egg hatches, and the *larvae* grow for one to three weeks before they *pupate*. The *pupae* rest for two or three weeks more. Then each one begins to *eclose*, breaking out of its cocoon as one of the *callows*, which are young adults.

162.title: Colony life cycle
162.text: A colony passes through three stages. In founding, the lone queen, after mating, chooses a site, lays her first eggs and raises the first workers herself. In growth, workers go out to *forage*, widen the tunnels and chambers and look after the *brood* in the queen's place, so she can concentrate on laying. In reproduction, the colony rears a batch of young queens and males, which depart to found colonies of their own, and the cycle begins again.

167.title: Ant facts 1
167.text:
Ants by the numbers
All the ants in the world together probably weigh about as much as all the people, or even more. Ants live in almost every land area, except the icy poles and the tops of high mountains. No other group of insects, and no other animal, has more individuals. Scientists have named more than twelve thousand kinds of ant. About half a million ants weigh a pound. Press Next for page 2.

168.title: Ant facts 2
168.text:
Ants are ancient
Ants are an old group of animals and have changed very little in tens of millions of years, much as sharks have.

Ants are strong
For their size ants are very strong. An ant can carry 10 to 20 times its own weight, and ants cooperate to move loads that are far too heavy for one. A group of ants may drag a dead beetle many times their size. Press Next for page 3.

169.title: Ant facts 3
169.text:
Ants are everywhere
Estimates run to about twenty million billion ants on Earth, which is millions of ants for every person. One huge connected supercolony on the Japanese island of Hokkaido holds hundreds of millions of workers. In tropical forests ants make up a large part of the animal life.

Ants live long
Among insects, ants are some of the longest-lived. Workers live about a year, and in some species four to five years. Queens can live for over twenty years. Press Top to return to the first page.

171.title: Game strategy
171.text: In the game you are the mind of the colony. You hop into and out of single ants and treat them as disposable instruments. Ants die in large numbers, sometimes even the one you are occupying, yet losing a single ant barely affects the colony. Press a name in the menu to read about seven topics.

172.title: Overall goals
172.text:
OpenSimAnt has three games.

Quick Game: your black colony competes with the red colony for food and land. The aim is to beat the reds by killing their queen. Spiders, ant lions, heavy rain, human feet and lawn mowers make it harder.

Full Game: the final goal is to take the house, and to clear the yard of red ants, by planting fresh colonies throughout the lawn. This needs *breeders*, the males and new queens, and mating (see the Full game card).

Experimental Game: you are a human experimenting with ants.

173.title: Gathering food
173.text: Gather as much as you can. Food is what new ants are made of: the amount of food sets your colony's health, and the colony's health sets its birth rate. Tips for *foraging*: run the yellow ant to a fresh find, *recruit* helpers on the spot and let them go, and they lift the food and haul it back. Or carry an item to the nest yourself, leaving a scent that pulls your ants towards the source. Whatever you take is lost to the red side.

174.title: Keyboard shortcuts
174.text:
Tab - swap the active window: Map or Edit
Backspace - stop the yellow ant, or centre the view on it
Alt + click - the same as a double-click
1 - recruit 5 ants
2 - recruit 10 ants
3 - release half of your recruits
4 - release all of them
X - exchange: jump into another ant
Alt + 2 - recruit every black ant
0 - alarm scent mode on or off
Right-click in the Map window - yellow ant commands
Ctrl + arrow keys - scroll the Edit window

175.title: Warfare
175.text: Attack the red colony only with more ants and better colony health than the enemy has. Fight in a soldier's body, since soldiers come out ahead more often. Lure the spider towards the enemy's nest. Raise the yellow ant's low-health alert threshold: it then halts to feed more often, but that makes it a stronger fighter. Guard the yellow ant during an advance. If it dies, you lose time while it is reborn, every ant it had recruited is set free and the attack ends.

176.title: Full game
176.text: The goal is to conquer the whole property, house and lawn, and to drive out the human residents. Victory comes from wiping out every red ant and controlling about 70 per cent of the house's patches. Choose the sites of new colonies with care: you need a route to the house, but you must also keep the reds contained. Patches you are not playing keep running in the background. A red colony hemmed in by black colonies on several sides falls more easily to a freshly founded colony.

178.title: Experimental game
178.text: This is a sandbox. It gives you tools and toys to set the ants loose on, such as mazes, chemicals and even insecticide. Food never appears by itself: you control all the food. Nothing counts as a win or a loss, so it is a good way to find out how ants cope with whatever you put in their way. Hold Alt while using a tool to remove things instead: the food tool puts food down, and with Alt held it picks food up again.
